questions.explain: The chapter's core principle is that runbooks generated from msdb (sysjobs, sysjobsteps, sysjobhistory) are evidence-based projections of live configuration, unlike wiki pages written from memory that rot.
options: Because msdb is backed up more frequently than the wiki
Because hand-written runbooks use the wrong Markdown dialect
Because msdb holds the live job definitions, steps, schedules, and execution history — so generated docs reflect reality instead of someone's recollection
Because the wiki cannot store T-SQL code blocks
questions.q: Why does the chapter insist the source of truth for runbooks is msdb, not the team wiki?

questions.explain: The 30-day rollup (avg duration, failure counts, last outcome) tells the on-call engineer what 'normal' looks like before deciding whether the current run is abnormal.
options: To satisfy auditors who require 30 days of logs
To show average duration, failure counts, and recent outcomes — giving on-call engineers a baseline for 'normal' behavior
To identify which jobs to delete for license savings
To calculate the exact cost of each job execution
questions.q: What is the operational purpose of including 30-day execution history in a generated runbook?

questions.explain: CHECKSUM_AGG over step definitions, schedules, and notification operators produces a fingerprint; recomputing it hourly and comparing to the stored value detects drift and triggers regeneration.
options: A CHECKSUM_AGG fingerprint over job steps, schedules, and notifications, recomputed on a schedule and compared to the value stored at generation time
A nightly full backup of the msdb database
A Slack reminder asking DBAs to review docs monthly
Comparing the runbook word count against the previous version
questions.q: How does the chapter recommend detecting runbook drift?

questions.explain: The auto-generated header marks the file as a projection of live config and warns that hand edits will be overwritten — preventing the worst outcome of generated docs that someone 'fixed' by hand and which then silently diverge.
options: It marks the file as auto-generated and warns that hand edits will be overwritten, preventing silent divergence
It improves the Markdown rendering speed
It satisfies a legal requirement for document headers
It encrypts the runbook contents
questions.q: What is the purpose of the auto-generated header comment in each runbook Markdown file?

questions.explain: The chapter requires every recommended step to cite at least two independent incidents where it was the actual resolution; one-off workarounds go in an 'observed once' appendix, preventing a single ticket's workaround from becoming recommended practice.
options: To only include incidents from the last 7 days
To require every recommended step to cite at least two independent incidents, with one-off workarounds relegated to an appendix
To delete all tickets older than one quarter before mining
To let the LLM invent plausible steps when tickets are sparse
questions.q: What evidence bar does the chapter set for incident-derived runbook steps?
